title: Ultimate Bishop
summary: Use a checking bishop sacrifice to interrupt the rook’s blockade and create two connected promotion threats.

nodes.question: How can White make both pawns count?
nodes.explanation: The rook on d2 stops the d7 pawn. Direct promotion lets it capture and leaves Black’s king able to collect the other pawn.

branches.title: Force the rook off the promotion file
commentary: Begin after ...Ke5. White’s bishop and two advanced connected pawns must defeat the rook’s blockade.
Bd6+ checks the king and interferes with the rook’s line to d7. Either capture changes the blockade.
Rxd6 removes the bishop and places the rook on d6. White can now create two promotion threats by advancing the e-pawn.
e7 makes two simultaneous promotion threats. Capturing d7 cannot stop e8=Q.
Rxd7 collects one pawn. This is the illustrated choice, not an assertion that Black has no other legal move.
e8=Q+ promotes with check. The saved tablebase confirms that this exact queen-versus-rook position with Black’s c-pawn is winning for White; conversion is not shown as an automatic capture.
branches.explanation: e8=Q+ promotes with check. The saved tablebase confirms that this exact queen-versus-rook position with Black’s c-pawn is winning for White; conversion is not shown as an automatic capture.

branches.title: The king takes the interfering bishop
commentary: The bishop sacrifice also works if Black uses the king to capture it.
Bd6+ offers the bishop while interrupting the rook’s d-file.
Kxd6 places Black’s own king between Rd2 and the d7 pawn.
d8=Q+ promotes with check because the rook cannot move through its king on d6. The resulting position is a checked White win.
branches.explanation: d8=Q+ promotes with check because the rook cannot move through its king on d6. The resulting position is a checked White win.

branches.title: Promote without interrupting the rook
commentary: Try the immediate promotion and compare what remains after exchanges.
d8=Q throws away the win. The rook still has a clear path up the d-file.
Bxd8 wins the rook back, but leaves the remaining white pawn exposed.
Kxe6 removes that pawn. White is left with a bishop against Black’s c-pawn; the exact ending is drawn with best play.

exercises.prompt: What changes when the rook takes the bishop on d6?
exercises.answer: The bishop disappears, but White gains e7 and two promotion threats. The rook can collect only one pawn in the illustrated continuation.

exercises.prompt: What changes when the king takes on d6?
exercises.answer: Black’s king blocks its own rook’s path up the d-file, allowing d8=Q+ immediately.

startContext: Begin after ...Ke5 at 134 seconds, once the earlier nine-piece setup has reduced to seven pieces. Earlier promotion and stalemate variations remain source context. The final bishop interference and its two capture responses are checked here.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
